GTYC vs. HYC (Caseville): historical wind

  1. HYC is the windier venue in September, and that holds up. After accounting for year-to-year variability, HYC averages +2.3 kt more than GTYC (CI +1.3 to +3.2) and has 11.8 points more of its racing hours in the 5–20 kt sweet spot (CI +4.6 to +20.1).
  2. The gap comes from light air. 37% of GTYC racing hours are below 5 kt against 25% at HYC. Neither venue has meaningful time at 20 kt or more in HRRR.
  3. GTYC is an afternoon-thermal venue. A 10 AM start catches the lightest part of the day, so later starts should help (see time of day).
  4. HYC’s mid-June window looks like September (8.9 vs 8.7 kt mean) but builds more through the afternoon.
  5. HRRR reads low against the buoys, so treat the raw numbers as a lower bound on wind. The venue ranking is the same either way; the absolute levels are not (see bias-adjusted range).
  6. Year-to-year variability dominates. September yearly means range 4.6–9.2 kt at GTYC and 5.0–12.3 kt at HYC.

Method

Wind comes from NOAA’s HRRR model (3 km analysis, 10 m wind), averaged over the water cells only in a ±4 nm box around a sample point offshore of each club. Statistics use racing hours 14–20 UTC (10 AM–4 PM EDT) over 2015–2025.

Correction, 20 Oct 2026: the first run measured GTYC’s bearing and distance from a club position that was about 1.9 nm too far south. The sample point moved north by the same amount and every GTYC figure was recomputed from the same cached data. HYC’s position was already correct (within 10 m). Conclusions are unchanged; GTYC’s mean rose 0.1 kt (6.3 to 6.4).

Speed bins: < 5 kt light, 5–20 kt sweet spot, ≥ 20 kt heavy. Usable day: at least 3 consecutive racing hours in 5–20 kt.

Wind direction is highly variable at both venues (steadiness R about 0.1–0.2). North is the most common quadrant in every window (37–40% of racing hours); HYC in September shows more westerly flow (29%).

GTYC, Sept 8–14. Wind rose (direction wind blows from), speed mix and statistics for racing hours, 2015–2025. Light air is the main shortfall, and HRRR shows essentially no hours at 20 kt or more.

HYC, Sept 8–14. Flow is mostly from the north through north-east and from the south-west to west; about three racing hours in four fall in the 5–20 kt sweet spot, and almost none reach 20 kt.

HYC, June 14–21. Similar to September in speed mix, with a slightly heavier tail (maximum 26.5 kt).

Scheduling implication. At GTYC the racing window straddles the ramp-up: the first hour averages 5.6 kt and the last 7.4 kt. Later first-gun times would likely improve GTYC’s light-air exposure. This report did not test other start times; the cached hourly data can.

Buoy winds are scaled to 10 m with a neutral log profile (about ×1.15). Raw and power-law (×1.23) versions are shown because this adjustment is the largest single uncertainty. HRRR vs buoy, racing hours. Dashed line is 1:1. HYC clusters close to the line; GTYC sits below it, and HRRR rarely produces the strong-wind events the buoy records.

Reading. HRRR gets the timing of wind changes right (HYC especially) but runs low, over-represents light air, and almost never produces heavy air. Directions are rotated by 10–15° on average. GTYC’s weaker correlation is consistent with a narrow bay that a 3 km grid represents with only a few water cells.

Bias-adjusted range

HRRR was quantile-mapped to the height-adjusted buoy winds (fitted per season on matched racing-hour pairs) and applied to the venue series. This is an adjustment, not a measurement: the truth likely lies between the raw and adjusted versions.

< 5 kt (light)5–20 kt (sweet spot)≥ 20 kt (heavy)

Share of racing hours by wind-speed bin. The ranking of venues does not change, but the adjusted figures shift hours out of light air and into the 5–20 kt range.

How much to trust the adjustment

  • GTYC (moderate confidence). The buoy is about 2 nm south of the sample point, in the same bay. The adjusted mean stayed between 8.0 and 8.35 kt across five fitting choices (quantile mapping on Sept only, Aug–Oct, or Sept+Oct, and two linear scalings). A cross-check fitted on one year and tested on the others predicted 8.28 vs an observed 8.39 kt (fit 2016) and 9.29 vs 8.65 kt (fit 2018). The figures above use the Sept-only fit.
  • HYC (treat as an upper bound). The buoy is 14 nm from the sample point in open bay, so the adjustment may overstate wind near the Caseville shore, particularly heavy air.
  • The adjusted HYC–GTYC gap is about 1.7–2.0 kt, so the ranking is unchanged.

Corrections to the earlier nine-venue proposal. Tawas Bay’s 17.3 kt maximum is not the lowest of the nine venues (Grand Traverse’s 16.4 kt is lower). The cause of the 476-observation HYC count was never identified; the stated explanation (six missing 2015 files) does not account for it. The same window now returns 523 racing hours for HYC, with all 16 missing hours in 2015–2018.

Caveats

  • HRRR is a 3 km model analysis, not an observation. It is low-biased against the buoys and handles narrow water poorly: GTYC’s West Arm is only 1–2 grid cells wide.
  • Buoy wind at 2.3–2.4 m must be scaled to 10 m. The result is sensitive to the method, and atmospheric stability is not modeled.
  • The GTYC buoy record is only 2016–2018, and the HYC buoy is 14 nm from the sample point.
  • Eleven seasons, one calendar week per year. Intervals are wide, and year-to-year differences are large (HYC’s September mean ranged from 5.0 to 12.3 kt).
  • Race-course layout, shoreline effects inside the bay, safety, logistics and fleet preferences are not captured.
